items.readable_text:
Content:
We can use set-builder notation to represent sets that lie in the coordinate plane.

Content:
For example, let's describe the following shaded region using set-builder-notation.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e9c62724d7bc01a7ad64b42e00e73f16]

Content:
First, notice that a point [MATH: P(x,y)] lies inside the rectangle if the following conditions are satisfied:

Content:
[MATH: 2 < x < 6, 2 < y < 5.]

Content:
However, notice that we also need to

Content:
- include the left edge ([MATH: x=2]), and
- include the right edge ([MATH: x=6]).

Content:
Therefore, we change the corresponding inequality symbols to non-strict, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 2≤x≤6, 2 < y < 5.]

Content:
Moreover, since every real value in these intervals is included, [MATH: x\in \mathbb R, y\in\mathbb R,] and therefore

Content:
[MATH: (x,y)\in \mathbb R\times\mathbb R = \mathbb R^2.]

Content:
Thus, we can write our set as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \Big\{
(x,y) \in \mathbb R^2
\: : \:

2
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq}
x
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq}
6,
\:
2
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\lt}
y
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\lt}
5
\Big\}.]

items.title: Describing Rectangular Sets Using Set-Builder Notation

sections.normalized_html: Describe the set of points shown above using set-builder notation.
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/9ec63ab02935633fe11a069f72b4098b]

Describe the set of points shown above using set-builder notation.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since all points [MATH: P(x,y)] in our set lie at integer values of [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we have [MATH: x\in \mathbb Z, y\in\mathbb Z,] and therefore

[MATH: (x,y)\in \mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z = \mathbb Z^2.]

The points [MATH: P(x,y)] satisfy the condition

[MATH: x \in \{1,2,3\}, \quad y \in \{ -3,-2,-1,0,1,2 \}.]

In other words,

[MATH: 1 \leq x \leq 3, \quad -3 \leq y \leq 2]

Therefore, we can write our set as follows:

[MATH: \Big\{ (x,y) \in \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathbb Z^2} \: : \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1} \leq x \leq \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}3} , \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-3} \leq y \leq \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2} \Big\}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since all points [MATH: P(x,y)] in our set lie at integer values of [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we have [MATH: x\in \mathbb Z, y\in\mathbb Z,] and therefore

[MATH: (x,y)\in \mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z = \mathbb Z^2.]

The points in our set include all those that lie below the line [MATH: y=x+2.] For those points, the following condition is satisfied:

[MATH: y \lt x+2]

Also, notice that some points in our set lie on the line. We include these points by changing the inequality symbol above as follows:

[MATH: y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq }x+2]

Therefore, we can write the set as follows:

[MATH: \Big\{(x,y) \in \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathbb Z ^2} \: : \: y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq }x+2 \Big\}]

items.title: Linear Boundaries, Two Conditions

sections.normalized_html: Describe the shaded region shown above using set-builder notation.
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/7cac8ef29134e3864a40c2aac8a76339]

Describe the shaded region shown above using set-builder notation.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The points in our set include all those that lie above the line [MATH: y=2x] and below the line [MATH: y=3.]

A point [MATH: P(x,y)] lies inside the shaded region if the following conditions are satisfied:

[MATH: y \gt 2x, \qquad y < 3.]

Combining this into a single condition, we have

[MATH: 2x \lt y < 3.]

We must also include the line [MATH: y= 3] since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the corresponding inequality symbol above as follows:

[MATH: 2x \lt y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq } 3]

Moreover, since we're considering every real value in this region, [MATH: x\in \mathbb R, y\in\mathbb R,] and therefore

[MATH: (x,y)\in \mathbb R\times\mathbb R = \mathbb R^2.]

Therefore, we can write the set as

[MATH: \Big\{(x,y)\in \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathbb R^2 } \: : \: 2x \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\lt } y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq } 3 \Big\}.]

key_prerequisites.name: Equations of Ellipses Centered at the Origin

sections.normalized_html: Use set builder notation to describe the shaded region given in the diagram below:
sections.readable_text:
Use set builder notation to describe the shaded region given in the diagram below:

[IMG: /graphics/fecea6c55850b5b4d4d702f2d38d5315]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length [MATH: a] and a vertical radius of length [MATH: b] is given by [MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1.]

Here, the elliptical boundary of our region has horizontal radius [MATH: a=5] and vertical radius [MATH: b=4.] Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is [MATH: (x^{2})/(25) + (y^{2})/(16)|= 1,] which we can write as [MATH: 16x^2 + 25y^2 = 400.]

We're interested in describing all points that lie outside the ellipse. So, let's pick any point outside the region, say, [MATH: (10,0).] Substituting its coordinates into the equation of the boundary, we obtain

[MATH: 16(10)^2+25(0)^2 \: {\color{blue}>} \: 400.]

As a result, the points [MATH: P(x,y)] in our region are any real numbers that satisfy the condition

[MATH: 16x^2 + 25y^2 \gt 400.]

We must also include the curve [MATH: 16x^2 + 25y^2 = 400] since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the inequality symbol above as follows:

[MATH: 16x^2 + 25y^2 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\geq } 400.]

Therefore, we can write the set as

[MATH: \Big\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \: : \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}16 }x^2 + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}25 }y^2 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\geq } 400 \bigg\}.]

[MATH: y \gt 2x, \qquad y < 3.]

Combining this into a single condition, we have

[MATH: 2x \lt y < 3.]

We must also include the line [MATH: y= 3] since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the corresponding inequality symbol above as follows:

[MATH: 2x \lt y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq } 3]

[MATH: (x,y)\in \mathbb R\times\mathbb R = \mathbb R^2.]

Therefore, we can write the set as

[MATH: \Big\{(x,y)\in \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathbb R^2 } \: : \: 2x \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\lt } y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq } 3 \Big\}.]

Item 11 — Example: Describing Non-Rectangular Sets Using Set-Builder Notation

Example Prompt:
Use set builder notation to describe the shaded region given in the diagram below:

[IMG: /graphics/fecea6c55850b5b4d4d702f2d38d5315]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length [MATH: a] and a vertical radius of length [MATH: b] is given by
[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1.]

Here, the elliptical boundary of our region has horizontal radius [MATH: a=5] and vertical radius [MATH: b=4.] Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is
[MATH: (x^{2})/(25) + (y^{2})/(16)|= 1,]
which we can write as
[MATH: 16x^2 + 25y^2 = 400.]

We're interested in describing all points that lie outside the ellipse. So, let's pick any point outside the region, say, [MATH: (10,0).] Substituting its coordinates into the equation of the boundary, we obtain

[MATH: 16(10)^2+25(0)^2 \: {\color{blue}>} \: 400.]

As a result, the points [MATH: P(x,y)] in our region are any real numbers that satisfy the condition

[MATH: 16x^2 + 25y^2 \gt 400.]

We must also include the curve [MATH: 16x^2 + 25y^2 = 400] since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the inequality symbol above as follows:

[MATH: 16x^2 + 25y^2 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\geq } 400.]

Therefore, we can write the set as

[MATH: \Big\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \: : \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}16 }x^2 + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}25 }y^2 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\geq } 400 \bigg\}.]
